entities.summary:
Cerdo, a Gnostic teacher active in Rome during the mid-2nd century CE, emerged from a Syrian background, likely during the reign of Emperor Antoninus Pius (138-161 CE). His theological contributions were instrumental in the development of dualistic Christian thought, particularly through his assertion of two distinct deities: a harsh, righteous God of the Old Testament responsible for creation and law, and a benevolent, merciful God of the New Testament who was the father of Jesus Christ. This radical theological framework challenged the emerging orthodox Christian understanding of a single, consistent divine being and significantly influenced subsequent Gnostic movements, most notably through his disciple Marcion.

Cerdo's teachings posited that the material world was inherently evil, created by the inferior Old Testament God, while salvation was offered by the superior New Testament God through a Christ who only appeared to have a physical body (docetism). He encouraged followers to reject the Old Testament entirely, viewing its scriptures as incompatible with the teachings of Christ. This theological schism, which he propagated in Rome, led to his eventual excommunication from the nascent Christian community, as recorded by early Church Fathers such as Irenaeus of Lyon and Tertullian, who vehemently opposed his doctrines.
